subject: science
title: KS3 Science - Working Scientifically: Scientific Investigation
description: Short KS3 reading passages on scientific investigation, variables, repeats, graphs, conclusions and evaluation. Each passage includes retrieval, inference and explanation questions for Working Scientifically revision.
subtitle: Reading practice on KS3 scientific investigation skills and evidence-based conclusions.

data.sourcePassage: A scientific investigation begins with a question that can be tested using evidence. A question such as how does temperature affect the time taken for sugar to dissolve is testable because temperature can be changed and dissolving time can be measured. A question such as is sugar interesting is not useful for a scientific investigation because it depends on personal opinion. In KS3 science, a good question often links an independent variable to a dependent variable. The investigator changes one factor, measures another factor, and keeps important control variables the same. This structure helps the results show whether the changed factor really affected the measurement.

questions.question: What kind of question begins a scientific investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: A testable question that can be answered using evidence.

questions.question: Which question is testable?
questions.modelAnswer: How does temperature affect dissolving time?
options: How does temperature affect dissolving time?

questions.question: Why is is sugar interesting not a useful scientific investigation question?
questions.modelAnswer: It depends on opinion rather than measurements or observations.

questions.question: What two variable types are linked in many good investigation questions?
questions.modelAnswer: The independent variable and the dependent variable.

questions.question: Explain why control variables help make a question easier to answer fairly.
questions.modelAnswer: They keep other important factors the same, so changes in the results are more likely to be caused by the independent variable.

data.sourcePassage: In a toy car ramp investigation, the question might be how does ramp height affect the distance a toy car travels? The independent variable is the ramp height because the investigator deliberately changes it. The dependent variable is the distance travelled because this is what is measured. Important control variables include the same toy car, same ramp surface, same starting position, same floor surface and same release method. The car should be released without pushing because a push would add an extra force. If a student changed the ramp height and also used a different car each time, the test would not be fair. The distance might change because of the car, not because of the ramp height.

data.sourcePassage: Repeats are measurements taken again using the same method. They help scientists see whether results are consistent and can make conclusions more reliable. A mean is an average found by adding repeat results and dividing by the number of results used. For example, the mean of 22 cm, 24 cm and 23 cm is 23 cm. An anomaly is a result that does not fit the pattern. Scientists should not delete an anomaly just because it is inconvenient. They should check what may have caused it, repeat the measurement if possible, and only exclude it if there is a clear reason. Repeats improve reliability, but they do not automatically make results accurate if the equipment or method is poor.

questions.question: What should a scientist do before excluding an anomaly?
questions.modelAnswer: Check for a clear cause and repeat the measurement if possible.

questions.question: Why do repeats not automatically make results accurate?
questions.modelAnswer: If the method or equipment is poor, repeated measurements can be consistent but still wrong.

data.sourcePassage: Results should be recorded clearly and honestly in a table. A good results table includes the independent variable in the first column, repeat readings in separate columns, a mean column when repeats are used, and units in the headings. Graphs help scientists see patterns. A line graph is usually used when the independent variable is continuous numerical data, such as temperature, time, length or voltage. A bar chart is usually used when the independent variable is a category, such as surface type or material. On a graph, the independent variable usually goes on the x-axis and the dependent variable usually goes on the y-axis. A best-fit line shows the overall trend and does not need to join every point.

questions.question: Why is a line graph suitable for temperature and dissolving time?

questions.question: Explain why a best-fit line should not simply join every point.
questions.modelAnswer: It should show the overall trend because real results may vary and some points may be anomalous.

data.sourcePassage: A conclusion answers the original question using evidence from the results. A strong conclusion describes the pattern, gives numerical evidence, and may include a scientific explanation. For example, a student might write that increasing ramp height increased the distance travelled, supported by mean distances at 10 cm and 50 cm. Evaluation is different. Evaluation judges the quality of the method. It should include a specific strength, weakness, effect on results and improvement. Writing human error is too vague. A better evaluation might explain that reaction time when stopping a stopwatch made times less precise, and suggest using a light gate or video timing. Good evaluations help scientists improve future investigations.

questions.question: Which evaluation is most specific?
questions.modelAnswer: Reaction time may have made stopwatch readings less precise.

questions.question: How could using a light gate improve a timing investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: It reduces the effect of human reaction time, making timing measurements more precise.
